newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Zedillo lashes out at opposition.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zedillo lashes out at opposition.

text.p: Celebrating 68 years of unbroken rule by his PRI party, President Ernesto Zedillo on Sunday lambasted the opposition, raising the political heat ahead of mid-term elections in July.

In festive mood ahead of the birthday of one of the world's longest-ruling parties, Zedillo, who had pledged when taking office to maintain a "healthy distance" from his Institutional Revolutionary Party, made clear where he stood now as election fever heated up.
"True change cannot come from opposition campaigns that only point to what according to them our party has done wrong," Zedillo said.

"True change cannot come from a populism that only looks backwards or from an egotistical and arrogant individualism," he added, clearly echoing some of the slurs PRI leaders have hurled at the party's two main challengers recently.
Describing the PRI as Mexico's "best political party", he urged it to be triumphant in the elections for the mayor of Mexico City and the lower house of Congress on July 6.

His support for his party was not unusual, but having promised a more open democracy in a country where the PRI has traditionally wielded almost complete power, his attack on its opponents was likely to raise hackles.

"I need the support of a vigorous, triumphant, majority PRI," he said, apparently recognising the threat faced by the party in holding the Congressional majority that it has enjoyed since its founding in 1929.

The PRI's 68th birthday does not fall until Tuesday, but the celebration was moved forward in a thinly-disguised attempt to steal the public relations thunder from Mexico's two main opposition parties.

On Sunday, both parties held gala gatherings in Mexico City to pick their candidates for the first election to rule Mexico City. The PRI picked its candidate last month. Previously the mayor has been hand-picked by the president.
Delegates of the conservative National Action Party (PAN) on Sunday overwhelmingly picked the party's popular ex-leader Carlos Castillo Peraza as its candidate for the capital.

On the left, the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) cast between its former presidential candidate Cuautemoc Cardenas and ex-party leader Porfirio Munoz Ledo. Results were not expected until late on Sunday.

Facing an uphill struggle to repeat the robust victories that have marked its decades in power, the PRI leadership has blackened the opposition with a vengeance this year, painting the right as neo-Nazis and the left as communists.

Since Zedillo took power in December 1994, the PRI has suffered its most serious loss of support ever, partly due to an economic crisis that erupted after Zedillo devalued the peso three weeks after taking office.

Last year, the economy staged an unexpectedly robust recovery, however, and both Zedillo and his party appeared optimistic on Sunday that this would mark an improvement in its fortunes at the ballot box.

"Now that the strategy is beginning to provide the (economic) results that we aimed for, the public will have to recognise the political responsibility ... with which the PRI supported what was certainly unpopular in the short term, but indispensable for Mexico's survival," Zedillo said.
According to opinion polls this weekend published by Reforma newspaper, Zedillo's popularity is at a two-year high, partly because Mexicans are more optimistic about their economic prospects.
A separate Reforma/Time Magazine poll on Sunday said 30 percent of Mexicans would vote for the PRI if elections were held now, against 24 percent who favoured the PAN and 12 percent for the PRD.
